title: Chapter 17: Concurrency and Asynchronous Programming
description: Reason about concurrency from ownership and happens-before guarantees. Learners reproduce races, separate atomicity from visibility, guard invariants with the appropriate primitive, propagate interruption and cancellation, compose CompletableFuture stages on controlled executors, use virtual threads for suitable blocking workloads, bound queues, and shut every executor down deliberately.

lessons.title: Threads, shared memory, races, visibility, and happens-before
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Threads, shared memory, races, visibility, and happens-before

## Concurrency exposes shared state
Two threads can both read counter=0, compute 1, and write 1; one increment is lost. count++ is a read-modify-write sequence even though it is one Java expression.
```java
Thread worker = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("worker"));
worker.start();
worker.join();
System.out.println("finished");
```
Place this in a method declaring InterruptedException. start schedules a separate execution; calling run directly executes on the caller. join waits for termination and provides visibility of the completed thread's actions.

## Visibility and ordering
Happens-before describes guaranteed visibility between actions, including monitor release/acquire, volatile write/read, thread start, and successful join. Observing a race “work” in repeated runs does not establish a guarantee. sleep is not synchronization.

## Practice
Implement two workers incrementing a shared counter, predict the ideal total, and explain a possible lost-update interleaving. Then confine each worker's total locally and combine after join. Distinguish concurrency from parallelism: overlapping progress does not require simultaneous CPU execution.

exercises.instructionMarkdown: Does Thread.sleep publish shared writes reliably?
choices: Yes; all caches flush during sleep
Yes; a longer sleep proves safety
No; sleeping is not a synchronization relationship
hints: Recall which actions establish happens-before edges (start, join, monitor release/acquire, volatile write/read) and notice sleep's absence from that list.

exercises.instructionMarkdown: Thread 1 locks accountA then waits for accountB; Thread 2 locks accountB then waits for accountA. What is the risk, and what practice from this lesson avoids it?

lessons.title: Executors, Callable, Future, interruption, cancellation, and shutdown
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Executors, Callable, Future, interruption, cancellation, and shutdown

## Own task execution and shutdown
```java
try (var pool = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {
    var result = pool.submit(() -> 6 * 7);
    System.out.println(result.get()); // 42
}
```
This Java 21 example uses ExecutorService as AutoCloseable. Callable returns a value and may throw; Future.get waits and can report ExecutionException or InterruptedException. A timeout on get limits the wait, not automatically the lifetime of the task; cancellation needs separate handling.

## Cooperative cancellation
Tasks should react to interruption during blocking calls or check interrupted status during long computations. Catching InterruptedException usually requires propagating it or restoring status with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). Swallowing it can defeat shutdown.

Pool size is not the only bound: common executor factories use queues that may grow without limit. Production submission needs queue/admission limits and a rejection policy. Closing an executor waits for work; tasks ignoring cancellation can delay shutdown.

## Practice
Submit a failing task and inspect the original cause through ExecutionException. Add a timeout, cancel outstanding work, and verify resources close. Explain who owns a supplied executor and why a helper should not unexpectedly shut down a caller-owned pool.

exercises.title: Executors, Callable, Future, interruption, cancellation, and shutdown: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Does Future.get(timeout) automatically stop the task on timeout?
choices: No; cancellation and task cooperation need separate handling
Yes; the worker is forcibly killed
Yes; its executor always shuts down
hints: Distinguish what happens to the caller waiting on get from what happens to the still-running task once that wait times out.

lessons.title: CompletableFuture composition, errors, timeouts, and executors
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# CompletableFuture composition, errors, timeouts, and executors

## Compose eventual results
```java
var result = java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> 21)
    .thenApply(n -> n * 2)
    .thenApply(Object::toString);
System.out.println(result.join()); // 42
```
thenApply transforms a value; thenCompose flattens a stage returning another future; thenCombine combines independent results. Non-async continuations may execute on the completing thread. Async methods without an explicit executor generally use the shared common pool.

## Failure and lifetime
exceptionally maps a failure to a fallback; handle sees both result and failure; whenComplete observes completion but can itself fail. Do not turn every error into a success value that conceals outages. join wraps exceptional completion in CompletionException.

Timeout completion and cancellation do not necessarily stop underlying I/O. Propagate deadlines to the actual operation and release its resources. Avoid blocking inside stages that need the same small executor to make progress.

## Practice
Combine two independent calculations and implement a dependent third using thenCompose. Inject one failure and prove which stages run. Provide an explicit executor, close it after completion, and explain the difference between observing an error and recovering from it.

lessons.title: Chapter 17 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 17 assessment

Apply this chapter's happens-before and ownership reasoning to the decision scenario, then repair **Restore interruption** with the same cooperative-cancellation discipline the executor, CompletableFuture, and virtual-thread lessons modeled. Write a prediction for what the broken interrupted-status check will report before running the debugger, and preserve the intended interruption contract when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the five lessons as well. Review the changed source for its contract, then explain the relevant tradeoff without consulting the answer.

choices: Cooperative cancellation and bounded lifecycle management

exercises.title: Join task results without shared mutation
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Implement parallelSum(int[] values). Submit one Callable<Integer> per supplied value to a Java 21 ExecutorService, collect all Future results, and return their sum. Input is non-null, has at most 1000 values, and the sum fits int. Close the executor; on interruption restore the interrupt and throw IllegalStateException with the cause; wrap other task failures with their cause. Automated tests verify results only: review executor ownership, actual submission, and cancellation behavior separately.
hints: Submit one Callable per array element before calling get on any Future, so all tasks are running concurrently rather than sequentially.
On InterruptedException, restore the interrupt with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and wrap it in IllegalStateException; unwrap other Future failures' causes before rethrowing.

exercises.title: Restore interruption
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the supplied defect so the program writes exactly `true`. The catch block currently swallows InterruptedException without restoring the interrupted status; preserve the surrounding try/catch structure while making the thread's interrupted flag observable again, and explain why your fix changes the result instead of hard-coding the print. Output tests verify the printed result; preserving the intended interruption contract requires reading the source, not just matching output.
hints: The catch must restore the interrupted status when it cannot propagate the exception.
